unit.name: Planning & Designing a Statistical Enquiry
unit.subtitle: From hypothesis to sampling plan — designing data collection that produces trustworthy answers.

lessons.title: Hypotheses, Questions and Investigation Constraints
lessons.description: Turning real-world curiosity into a testable hypothesis and managing the practical constraints of an enquiry.
lessons.content_html:
From Curiosity to Question

Every statistical investigation begins with a question someone wants to answer. A teacher wonders whether students who sleep longer perform better in tests. A public health team asks whether exercise frequency is linked to reported wellbeing. A market researcher wants to know whether younger shoppers spend more online than older ones. In each case, the curiosity is real — but curiosity alone is not enough. Statistics demands that you turn your question into something testable.

A hypothesis is a precise, testable statement — not a vague hunch. Compare these two versions of the same idea:

  • Vague question: “Do students who sleep more do better?”
  • Testable hypothesis: “Students who sleep eight or more hours per night will score higher on a memory test than students who sleep fewer than eight hours.”

The second version names the variables, states a direction, and makes clear what data you would need to collect. That precision matters because your entire investigation — what data to gather, how to sample, which statistical tools to use, and how to judge whether your results support or refute your prediction — flows from the hypothesis you write at the start.

Key Fact

A testable hypothesis names the variables involved, states a predicted relationship or difference, and can be supported or refuted through data. The specification does not require formal null-hypothesis notation — a clearly worded statement is sufficient.

Why Hypotheses Can Only Be Tested Through Data

It is tempting to think that a well-reasoned argument can “prove” a hypothesis. Statistics says no. You can believe something is true for entirely logical reasons and still be wrong when the data is collected. A hypothesis can only be tested through the appropriate collection and analysis of data — this is a core principle of the specification. Opinion, intuition, and personal experience are starting points for forming a hypothesis, not evidence for evaluating one.

This is why the design of an investigation matters so much. If your data collection is flawed — biased sample, poorly worded questions, or measurement error — then your conclusion, however confidently stated, rests on shaky foundations.

Investigation Constraints

Real investigations face practical limits. The specification lists five main types of constraint you should be able to discuss: time constraints, cost constraints, ethical issues, confidentiality concerns, and convenience.

Time: A survey conducted over one week gives a very different result from one run over a full year. If you are studying seasonal behaviour — ice cream sales, flu cases, holiday bookings — and your budget only allows one month of data collection, your results may not reflect the full picture.

Cost: A large random sample is statistically ideal but expensive. Interviewing participants in person is richer than an online questionnaire but far costlier. Many investigators compromise on sample size or method because of limited funds, and this affects the conclusions they can draw.

Ethical issues: Investigations involving human participants must not cause harm, distress, or embarrassment. Researching sensitive topics — mental health, financial hardship, relationship difficulties — requires careful handling. Participants must give their consent, and the researcher must decide whether the benefit of the knowledge outweighs any risk of harm.

Confidentiality: Data collected about individuals must be protected. If people fear that their personal information will be shared or used against them, they may refuse to participate or give dishonest answers. Guaranteeing anonymity — not attaching names to responses — typically improves both response rates and honesty.

Convenience: Sometimes the ideal population is simply not accessible. A researcher wanting to survey a random sample of all UK secondary school students faces enormous logistical challenges. Convenience shapes who can realistically be included.

A research question asks something open-ended: “Is there a relationship between screen time and sleep quality?” That is a useful starting point, but it is not a hypothesis.

A hypothesis makes a specific, directional prediction: “Students who spend more than three hours on screens per evening will report fewer hours of sleep than students who spend less than one hour on screens.” Now you know exactly what to measure, how to group participants, and what a supporting result would look like.

In the exam, if a question asks you to “write a hypothesis” and you write a question instead, you will lose marks. Make sure your answer is a statement, not a question.

Proactive Strategies: Planning for Problems

Good investigators do not just hope that problems will not arise — they plan for them. The specification expects you to know what kinds of problems can occur during an enquiry and how to mitigate them before they happen. Three common challenges are: difficulty identifying the population, non-response, and unexpected outcomes.

Identifying the population: For some investigations, the population is easy to define — all Year 11 students in a school, for example. For others, the boundary is blurry. If you want to study “regular gym users”, what counts as regular? Once per week? Five times per week? Defining the population clearly before you begin prevents disputes about who should have been included later.

Non-response: If a large proportion of people choose not to respond to your questionnaire, the results may be biased. Those who respond might systematically differ from those who do not. For example, people with strong opinions tend to respond at higher rates than those with moderate views. Strategies to reduce non-response include: keeping questionnaires short, offering an incentive, and following up with reminders.

Unexpected outcomes: Real data surprises you. A value that seems impossibly large might be a genuine outlier, a data entry error, or evidence that your hypothesis needs refinement. A good investigator builds in a review stage rather than assuming everything will go to plan.

Key Fact

Proactive strategies — such as piloting the questionnaire, offering anonymity, defining the population precisely, and building in a follow-up for non-responders — reduce the risk that problems discovered later will invalidate the entire investigation.

A student wants to test whether students who travel more than 30 minutes to school are more likely to arrive late than those who travel fewer than 30 minutes.

Hypothesis: “Students with a commute of more than 30 minutes will have a higher rate of late arrivals than students with a commute of fewer than 30 minutes.”

Constraints identified:

  • Time — data collection limited to one half-term; seasonal effects (e.g. winter delays) not captured.
  • Ethical — lateness data is sensitive; consent needed from school and parents for under-16s.
  • Non-response — some students may not return the travel-time form; a follow-up reminder planned.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘Explain’ and ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about investigation design, always link your answer to the specific scenario in the question. Writing “it could be biased” scores nothing — you must say which group is under-represented and why that matters for the conclusion. For a hypothesis-writing question, check that your answer is a statement (not a question), names the variables, and states a direction or predicted difference. Missing any of these typically costs a mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A hypothesis is a specific, testable statement predicting a relationship or difference between variables — it can only be confirmed or refuted through appropriate data collection and analysis, never by argument alone.
  • Real investigations face five main types of constraint: time, cost, ethical issues, confidentiality, and convenience — each can affect the sample size, method, and conclusions.
  • Proactive strategies — piloting, guaranteeing anonymity, defining the population precisely, and planning for non-response — reduce the risk of problems that invalidate an enquiry after data collection has begun.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a testable hypothesis rather than a research question?
A) Does diet affect academic performance?
B) Students who eat breakfast every day will score higher on concentration tests than students who skip breakfast.
C) What is the relationship between exercise and mood?
D) There might be a link between sleep and exam results.
practice_questions.marks: B [1 mark] — Only option B is a specific, testable statement with named variables and a predicted direction.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to investigate whether students who cycle to school report higher levels of physical fitness than those who travel by bus. Give two constraints that could affect the design of this investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any two of the following, up to 2 marks:
- Time constraint: data collection at one point in the year may not reflect behaviour in winter months.
- Cost constraint: fitness assessments (e.g. measured tests) may be expensive; questionnaire-only alternatives are cheaper but less valid.
- Ethical constraint: asking participants about health or fitness may be sensitive; parental consent required for under-16s.
- Convenience constraint: the sample is limited to one school's students, so results may not generalise.
- Non-response: students may refuse to disclose travel method or fitness level.

practice_questions.text:
A student writes the following hypothesis for a statistical investigation: 'There is a relationship between the amount of revision a student does and their test score.'
Explain one way this hypothesis could be improved to make it more suitable for a statistical investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct improvements, each with a clear reason linking to how the improvement makes the hypothesis testable.
- The hypothesis does not name a direction: a better version would state 'Students who revise more than 5 hours per week will score higher than those who revise fewer than 2 hours per week' — this tells the investigator what a supporting result looks like.
- 'Amount of revision' is not operationalised: a better version would specify hours per week, sessions per day, or similar measurable quantity — this makes the variable possible to collect consistently.
Secure: One developed improvement with a clear reason.
Developing: Identifies an improvement but the reason is vague (e.g. 'so it is clearer').
Emerging: Restates the hypothesis without identifying a genuine improvement.

practice_questions.text:
A health researcher wants to investigate the link between screen time and reported headache frequency in teenagers. She plans to post questionnaires to 500 randomly selected households and ask the parent to pass it to their teenage child.
Suggest and justify two proactive strategies she could use to reduce problems before data collection begins.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each valid strategy and 1 mark for a justification that refers to a specific problem it addresses, up to 5 marks total (one strategy may score 2 marks if the justification is developed).
Mastering: Two strategies, each with a justification linked to a named problem (non-response, sensitivity, measurement inconsistency, or population definition).
- Offer anonymity and emphasise confidentiality in the covering letter [1] because teenagers may under-report screen time or headache frequency if they fear their parents will see the results, which would bias the data towards lower values [1].
- Run a pilot study on a small group of 10–15 students [1] to identify whether the screen-time question is interpreted consistently — if students differ in whether they count passive TV watching, the variable will be measured differently across participants, introducing random error [1].
- Include a prepaid return envelope or online completion option [1] to reduce non-response, because households that do not return the questionnaire may include those with the highest screen time (who have less time for other activities), biasing the sample [1].
Secure: Two strategies with partial justifications.
Developing: One strategy with a justification, or two strategies without justifications.
Emerging: One strategy without a justification.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a research question and a hypothesis, using an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Clear distinction with a specific example that illustrates both forms.
- A research question asks what the relationship might be (open-ended, e.g. 'Is there a link between exercise and mental health?') whereas a hypothesis is a specific, directional, testable statement (e.g. 'Students who exercise three or more times a week will report lower stress scores than those who exercise once or less per week') [2].
- The key feature of a hypothesis is that it specifies both variables and a predicted direction, so the investigator knows in advance what data would confirm or refute it [2].
Secure: Identifies the distinction with a partial example.
Developing: Identifies one feature without contrasting the two forms.
Emerging: Describes only one of the two forms.

practice_questions.text:
A student investigation team plan to study whether students in higher year groups spend more money per week than those in lower year groups. They decide to post their questionnaire on the school's social media page and analyse all responses received.
Discuss the limitations of this investigation design, including at least two different stages of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for identified limitations with developed explanations, up to 6 marks.
Mastering: At least two distinct limitations at different SEC stages, each with a developed explanation of why it weakens the conclusions. A final evaluative comment addresses whether the results can be trusted.
- Hypothesis/planning stage: 'higher year groups' and 'lower year groups' are not operationalised — without specifying which years are being compared, the investigator cannot stratify the sample meaningfully [1+1].
- Data collection stage: posting on social media means only students who follow the page and choose to respond will complete the survey — this is opportunity sampling, not random sampling, so the sample is likely biased towards students who are more active on social media, potentially those who spend more money [1+1].
- Data processing stage: self-reported spending is prone to recall bias and social desirability bias — students may under- or overestimate weekly spend depending on what they think is expected [1+1].
- Evaluation: the combination of biased sampling and self-report measurement error means the conclusions about spending differences between year groups cannot be reliably generalised to all students [1].
Secure: Two limitations identified, one developed.
Developing: One limitation with partial development.
Emerging: Names a limitation without explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a hypothesis in statistics?
options: A question that asks what the researcher wants to find out
A specific, testable statement predicting a relationship or difference between variables
A summary of the data collected during an investigation
A conclusion drawn after analysing the results

knowledge_checks.q: Why might non-response bias an investigation into students' revision habits?
options: Because non-respondents will have identical revision habits to respondents
Because students who revise the most are the most likely to have time to respond
Because students who revise least may be less motivated to complete the questionnaire, making the sample unrepresentative
Because non-response only affects investigations with very large samples

knowledge_checks.q: A hypothesis can only be tested through the appropriate _____ and analysis of data.
Guaranteeing _____ in a questionnaire typically improves both response rates and the honesty of answers on sensitive topics.
Match each investigation constraint to its description:
right: Limited data collection period may miss seasonal patterns
The investigation must not cause harm or distress to participants
The ideal population may not all be realistically accessible

glossary_terms.definition: A specific, testable statement that predicts a relationship or difference between variables, which can be supported or refuted through data collection and analysis.
A restriction on a statistical investigation caused by limited time available for data collection or analysis.
A restriction on a statistical investigation caused by limited financial resources, affecting sample size, equipment, or access to participants.
The situation where some members of a sample do not respond to a questionnaire or interview, which can introduce bias if non-respondents share a common characteristic.

lessons.title: Types of Data and Variables
lessons.description: Classifying data: quantitative, qualitative, discrete, continuous, bivariate and the explanatory/response variable pair.
lessons.content_html:
Why Classifying Data Matters

Before you can choose a graph, a formula, or a statistical test, you need to know what type of data you have. A bar chart is right for some data but completely wrong for others. The mean makes sense for some measurements but is meaningless for others. Every decision in the rest of your investigation flows from the type of data you collected. Getting this classification right at the start prevents wasted effort later.

Quantitative and Qualitative Data

Quantitative data is data that takes numerical values. Height in centimetres, temperature in degrees, number of goals scored — all of these are quantitative because you can do arithmetic with them. Calculating the mean height or the total goals scored is meaningful.

Qualitative data describes qualities or categories. Eye colour, favourite genre of music, a person’s opinion expressed in their own words — these are qualitative. You cannot calculate a meaningful mean eye colour. Qualitative data is often ‘words’ rather than numbers, though it can be coded into numbers (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree) — but even then, the codes are labels, not measurements.

Key Fact

The key test: can you do meaningful arithmetic with the values? If yes, the data is quantitative. If no (e.g. averaging “nationalities” makes no sense), it is qualitative.

Categorical and Ordinal Data

Within qualitative data, two further types matter. Categorical data falls into groups with no natural ordering. Blood group (A, B, AB, O), country of birth, and make of car are categorical — there is no sensible way to say that blood group B comes ‘after’ blood group A.

Ordinal data can be ordered or ranked, but the gaps between positions are not equal. Placing first, second, or third in a race is ordinal — you know the order, but ‘first is better than second’ does not tell you by how much. Survey responses such as “poor / fair / good / excellent” are ordinal: the order is clear, but the step from ‘poor’ to ‘fair’ is not necessarily the same size as the step from ‘good’ to ‘excellent’.

Discrete and Continuous Data

Within quantitative data, two further types are essential. Discrete data can only take specific, separate values. The number of students in a class is discrete: you can have 28 or 29 students, but not 28.4. The number of goals in a match is discrete.

Continuous data can take any value within a range. Height, weight, temperature, and time are all continuous — a student’s height could theoretically be 163.47 cm. In practice, measurement tools limit the precision, but the underlying characteristic is continuous.

Why does this distinction matter? Discrete data is usually represented with bar charts and pictograms (with gaps between bars). Continuous data is represented with histograms (no gaps), or can be grouped into class intervals. You should choose the representation that matches the data type, not the one that looks nicest.

Students often argue about shoe size. In the UK, shoe sizes come in specific values (6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, ...) — there is no UK size 7.3. That makes shoe size discrete, even though it is a numerical measurement.

Contrast this with foot length in centimetres. That is continuous — a foot could be 26.2 cm or 26.25 cm. The key question is whether the measuring system has genuine gaps between values, or whether it is just rounding a continuous thing. Shoe sizes are a labelling convention, so they are discrete. Foot lengths are continuous.

Ungrouped and Grouped Data

Data can also be described as ungrouped (individual values listed separately) or grouped (values collected into class intervals). Grouping is useful when a dataset is large and spread over a wide range — it makes patterns easier to see. However, grouping loses precision: once data is grouped, you can only estimate the mean, not calculate it exactly.

When creating class intervals, check that they do not overlap and that they cover the full range of the data. The choice of class width affects how clearly the distribution is visible: too many narrow classes and the pattern is obscured by noise; too few wide classes and important detail is lost.

Explanatory and Response Variables

When an investigation explores whether one thing influences another, statisticians distinguish between two types of variable. The explanatory variable (also called the independent variable) is the one the researcher believes causes or predicts changes. The response variable (also called the dependent variable) is the outcome being measured.

Example: if you investigate whether daily revision time influences exam score, then revision time is the explanatory variable and exam score is the response variable. Plotting on a scatter graph, convention places the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response variable on the vertical axis.

Key Fact

The explanatory variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis. The response variable goes on the vertical (y) axis. A memory cue: you explain how x causes changes in y.

Bivariate Data

Bivariate data is data where two measurements are taken on each individual. When you record both a student’s revision hours and their exam score, you have bivariate data — one pair of values per student. Bivariate data is used to investigate relationships: is there a correlation? Does the explanatory variable predict the response variable?

Multivariate Data (Higher)

Multivariate data is data where three or more variables are recorded for each individual. A researcher studying student performance might record revision hours, sleep duration, and exam score for each student — that is multivariate. Multivariate datasets are more realistic than bivariate ones, because real-world outcomes rarely have just a single influence.

The challenge with multivariate data is distinguishing the effect of one variable from the effects of others. If students who revise more also sleep more, it becomes difficult to say whether the exam improvement is due to revision, sleep, or both. This is why large data sets and statistical controls matter in real research.

Sometimes a questionnaire produces too many small categories. If ten students rate their commute as “less than 5 minutes”, thirty as “5–10 minutes”, and two as “50–60 minutes”, the very small categories make charts hard to read and comparisons unreliable.

Merging categories — such as combining “less than 5 minutes” and “5–10 minutes” into “up to 10 minutes” — can make the data more useful. The trade-off is that you lose detail. A good class interval choice balances readability with preserving the shape of the distribution.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘State/Name’ questions that ask you to classify data, be precise: do not write “numerical” when the answer is “discrete” or “continuous”. The examiner is testing whether you know the specific term. For ‘Explain’ questions, a common error is saying “discrete data has whole numbers” — this is nearly always true but not the definition. The definition is that discrete data can only take specific separate values. Shoe sizes are discrete but include halves. On questions about explanatory and response variables, always state which axis each goes on — this earns the method mark even if you misidentify which variable is which.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Quantitative data takes numerical values; qualitative data describes categories or qualities — the key test is whether meaningful arithmetic can be performed.
  • Discrete data takes only specific separate values (e.g. number of goals); continuous data can take any value within a range (e.g. height in cm). This distinction determines which graphical representations are appropriate.
  • The explanatory (independent) variable goes on the horizontal axis; the response (dependent) variable goes on the vertical axis — bivariate data records both for each individual to investigate relationships.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher records the following for each participant in a study: their age in years, whether they own a pet (yes/no), and the number of times they visited a GP in the past year.
Which of these variables is qualitative?
A) Age in years
B) Whether they own a pet
C) Number of GP visits
D) All three are quantitative
practice_questions.marks: B [1 mark] — Pet ownership (yes/no) is qualitative categorical data. Age and GP visits are quantitative.

practice_questions.text:
State whether each of the following is discrete or continuous data.
(a) The number of text messages sent by a student in one day.
(b) The time, in minutes, taken to complete a maths test.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Discrete [1 mark] — the number of texts can only be a whole number; there are no intermediate values.
(b) Continuous [1 mark] — time can take any value within a range, including fractions of a minute.

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates whether the distance a student lives from school affects the number of days they are absent per year. She plots a scatter graph and draws a line of best fit.
Write down which variable is the explanatory variable and which is the response variable. Explain which axis each should be plotted on.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct identification and 1 mark for each correct axis assignment, up to 4 marks.
Explanatory variable: distance from school [1 mark] — plotted on the horizontal (x) axis [1 mark].
Response variable: number of days absent [1 mark] — plotted on the vertical (y) axis [1 mark].
Accept 'independent variable' for explanatory and 'dependent variable' for response.

practice_questions.text:
A survey asks students to rate their enjoyment of school on a scale: poor / fair / good / excellent.
State the type of data this produces and explain one limitation of this data type for statistical analysis.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Correct data type with a precisely explained limitation.
- Type: ordinal data [1 mark] — the responses have a clear order but the gaps between categories are not necessarily equal [1 mark].
- Limitation: because the intervals are unequal, calculating the mean is not meaningful — the mean of 'poor' and 'excellent' depends on how you code them numerically, which is arbitrary [2 marks].
Secure: Correct type; limitation stated but not developed.
Developing: Names a broad category (qualitative/categorical) without identifying ordinal.
Emerging: Describes the scale without classifying it.

practice_questions.text:
A health researcher collects the following data for each participant: their age, their gender, their daily step count, their average nightly sleep in hours, and their self-rated health score (1–10).
Suggest and justify why this dataset should be described as multivariate rather than bivariate.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for identifying that more than two variables are recorded per person, and up to 4 further marks for a justified explanation.
Mastering: Clear statement that multivariate data records three or more variables per individual [1], with justification that explains the analytical advantage or distinction from bivariate [up to 4].
- Five variables are recorded for each participant (age, gender, step count, sleep, health score) [1].
- Bivariate data only records two variables per individual, allowing analysis of one pairwise relationship (e.g. sleep and health score) [1].
- Multivariate data allows investigation of how multiple explanatory variables interact — for example, whether both step count and sleep independently predict health score, or whether the effect of one disappears when the other is controlled for [1+1].
- This reflects more realistic conditions where outcomes have multiple influences [1].
Secure: Correct identification with partial justification.
Developing: States the number of variables without explaining what multivariate means.
Emerging: Confuses bivariate and multivariate.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether it is always possible to give a clear classification of data as either quantitative or qualitative. Use examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion with examples and a judgement.
Mastering: Two or more examples where classification is clear, at least one example where classification is ambiguous, and a concluding judgement.
- Clear quantitative: weight in kg, temperature in Celsius — arithmetic operations are clearly meaningful [1+1].
- Clear qualitative: eye colour, nationality — no meaningful average can be computed [1+1].
- Ambiguous: Likert scale responses (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) — these are coded numbers but the gaps between them are not equal, so treating them as quantitative is controversial; statisticians disagree on this [1+1].
- Judgement: classification is usually straightforward, but coded qualitative data creates genuine ambiguity that requires a decision about what analysis is appropriate [1].
Secure: Two contrasting examples with partial development.
Developing: One example with limited analysis.
Emerging: Defines quantitative and qualitative without using examples.

glossary_terms.definition: Data that can be measured or counted and expressed as a number.
Data that describes qualities or categories and cannot be meaningfully expressed as a number.
Data that falls into distinct named groups with no natural order between them.
Data where values can be placed in a meaningful order or rank, but the gaps between positions are not necessarily equal.
Quantitative data that can only take specific, separate values with no intermediate values possible.
Quantitative data that can take any value within a range, including fractions and decimals, limited only by the precision of measurement.
The variable that is thought to influence or explain changes in another variable; also called the independent variable.
The variable that is measured or observed and is expected to change in response to the explanatory variable; also called the dependent variable.
Data where two variables are recorded for each individual, allowing the investigation of a possible relationship between them.
Data where three or more variables are recorded for each individual, allowing the investigation of more complex relationships among multiple variables.

lessons.content_html:
Where Does Data Come From?

Every statistical investigation needs data — but that data has to come from somewhere. The two fundamental categories are primary data and secondary data. Understanding the difference between them — and knowing the advantages and limitations of each — is essential when planning an investigation and when evaluating someone else’s research.

Primary Data

Primary data is collected first-hand, specifically for your investigation. The main methods include:

  • Experimental: The researcher controls conditions to test a cause-and-effect relationship. A laboratory experiment removes external influences (high level of control). A field experiment takes place in a natural setting, which improves realism but reduces control. A natural experiment observes what happens when conditions change for non-research reasons — for example, observing the effect of a new bus route on school attendance rates.
  • Simulation: Uses models (often computer-based) to generate data when real-world collection is impossible or unethical — for example, simulating traffic patterns or the spread of an infectious disease.
  • Questionnaire: A set of written questions completed by participants. Cheap and scalable, but dependent on honest responses.
  • Observation: Watching and recording behaviour directly. Can capture what people actually do rather than what they say they do, but observer presence can influence behaviour.

Primary data has a major advantage: it is collected specifically for your purpose, so it should measure exactly what you need. The disadvantage is that it takes time and resources to collect.

Secondary Data

Secondary data already exists. Sources include published statistical databases, government censuses, academic studies, media reports, and reference publications. In the UK, organisations such as the Office for National Statistics (ONS), NHS Digital, the Met Office, and the Department for Education all publish large, high-quality datasets that researchers can use without collecting any data themselves.

The advantages of secondary data are significant: it is fast to access, often covers large populations, and may span decades of historical records that no individual researcher could replicate. The ONS Census, for example, covers the entire UK population at ten-year intervals — a dataset of that scale is simply not achievable through primary collection for most researchers.

However, secondary data has limitations. It was collected for a different purpose, so it may not measure exactly what you need. Variable definitions may differ — what counts as “unemployed” changed in UK statistics several times between the 1970s and 1990s, making long-run comparisons tricky. You also need to acknowledge the source of any secondary data you use, as the specification requires.

Key Fact

Secondary data: advantages — fast to access, large sample sizes, historical depth. Limitations — may not measure exactly what you need, variable definitions may have changed, source must be acknowledged and its quality assessed.

Census vs Sample

A census collects data from every member of the population. The UK Census, conducted every ten years, aims to record information about every household. A census gives complete data with no sampling error, but it is expensive, time-consuming, and in some cases impossible (not every person can be reached).

In contrast, sampling involves collecting data from a carefully chosen subset. Most practical investigations use samples. The challenge is making the sample representative enough that conclusions about the population are valid.

Reliability and Validity

These two words are used precisely in statistics and are often confused. Reliability is about consistency: does the measurement give the same result every time you use it? Validity is about accuracy of purpose: does the measurement capture the thing you actually want to know about?

A useful way to see the difference: imagine a bathroom scale that always reads 3 kg too heavy. It is reliable — it gives a consistent reading every time — but it is not valid for measuring your true weight. Conversely, asking students “How healthy do you feel?” on a scale of 1–10 might produce variable answers from the same student on different days (poor reliability) and may not accurately capture their clinical health status (poor validity).

Students frequently write “the data is reliable and valid” as if the two words mean the same thing, or they use one when they mean the other. In the exam, using these terms imprecisely will cost marks.

If a question asks about reliability, focus on: would repeated measurements give the same result? If it asks about validity, focus on: does the measurement actually capture what you want to measure? A questionnaire asking about income to proxy for social class is valid if income correlates well with social class — but only reliable if the same person answers the same question consistently across administrations.

Bias and Sensitivity

Bias is a systematic error — it pushes results in one direction rather than producing random noise. Bias can arise from: the way a sample is selected (sampling bias), the way questions are worded (response bias), or the sensitivity of the topic being researched.

Sensitive topics — income, health, political views, personal relationships — are particularly prone to response bias. People may give socially desirable answers rather than honest ones, or they may refuse to answer at all (non-response bias). When the people who refuse to answer share a characteristic relevant to the investigation, this creates a systematic distortion in the results.

Level of Control and Minimising Data Distortion (Higher)

In a controlled experiment, the researcher manipulates one variable (the explanatory variable) and keeps all others constant, so that any change in the response variable can be attributed to the manipulation. The level of control refers to how completely the investigator can hold other variables constant.

High control (laboratory experiments) makes causation easier to claim but may reduce ecological validity — the results may not apply to real-world settings. Low control (natural experiments, observational studies) reflects real-world conditions better but makes it harder to isolate cause and effect because other variables are free to vary.

Extraneous variables — variables that influence the response variable but are not the focus of the investigation — must be identified and managed. Techniques include controlling them directly (holding them constant across all participants), including a control group (a group that receives no treatment, against which the experimental group is compared), and randomisation (randomly assigning participants to groups so that extraneous variables are spread evenly).

Key Fact

Reliability = consistency across repeated measurements. Validity = the measurement captures what it is supposed to measure. A data source can be one without the other.

The specification explicitly states that secondary data sources should be acknowledged. In practice, this means recording where the data came from, when it was collected or published, and who collected it. This matters for two reasons.

First, it allows the reader to check the original source and assess its quality. A statistic from a government body such as the ONS is more likely to be reliable than one from a company’s own press release. Second, without acknowledgement, using someone else’s data without credit is a form of academic misconduct. In professional statistical work and in your investigation write-up, always note the source.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘Explain’ questions asking you to evaluate a data source, always link reliability and validity to the specific method described in the question. Saying “questionnaires are not always reliable” earns no marks — you need to say why this specific questionnaire on this specific topic may produce inconsistent or inaccurate results. Sensitivity of the topic is often the key reason: if the topic is sensitive (e.g. income, health), responses are more likely to be incomplete or biased. On ‘Discuss’ questions, always present both advantages and limitations before reaching a judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary data is collected first-hand for the specific investigation; secondary data already exists and was collected by someone else for a different purpose — both have advantages and limitations that must be evaluated in context.
  • Reliability means consistency of measurement across repeated applications; validity means the measurement captures the construct it is supposed to measure — these are different properties and a measure can have one without the other.
  • Bias arises when systematic errors push results in one direction; sensitivity of the topic is a common source of response bias and non-response, which distorts conclusions if not managed proactively.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of secondary data?
A) A student conducts a survey of her classmates' screen time.
B) A researcher observes shoppers in a supermarket and records their behaviour.
C) A student downloads data about UK birth rates from the Office for National Statistics website.
D) A science class measures the reaction times of 30 volunteers.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — Data downloaded from the ONS was collected by someone else for a different purpose and already exists, making it secondary data.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher measures the resting heart rate of a sample of students on Monday, then measures the same students again on Wednesday under identical conditions, and gets almost the same values.
State whether this suggests the measurement is reliable, valid, or both. Give a reason for your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Reliable [1 mark] because the measurement gives consistent results when repeated under the same conditions [1 mark].
Note: this does not tell us about validity — it could still be an inaccurate proxy for cardiovascular health.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using secondary data from a government census for a statistical investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each point clearly stated, up to 3 marks.
Advantage: the census covers the entire population, giving a very large dataset with no sampling error [1].
Disadvantage (any one of the following):
- The data was collected for a different purpose, so it may not measure exactly what the current investigation needs [1].
- Variable definitions may have changed between census years, making long-run comparisons unreliable [1].
- The census is conducted infrequently (every ten years), so it may not reflect current conditions [1].

practice_questions.text:
A school wants to investigate whether students who eat a hot lunch report higher energy levels in afternoon lessons than those who eat a packed lunch. A teacher designs a questionnaire where students rate their energy level on a scale of 1 to 10.
Explain one reason why this measurement method may lack validity for this investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Validity issue identified and clearly linked to why the measurement does not capture what is being studied.
- A self-rated energy score on a 1-10 scale may not validly measure actual energy levels [1] because students may interpret ‘energy’ differently (physical tiredness vs motivation vs alertness), so the scale does not consistently capture the same construct across participants [1].
- The measurement is susceptible to demand characteristics [1]: students may give a higher score if they know the teacher believes hot lunches are better, not because their energy is actually higher [1].
Secure: Validity issue identified with partial development.
Developing: Raises reliability or bias without correctly addressing validity.
Emerging: States the questionnaire is ‘not accurate’ without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
A university researcher wants to investigate the link between social media use and self-reported wellbeing in teenagers. She plans to use secondary data from a published government survey.
Suggest and justify two limitations of using this secondary data for her investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each limitation and 1 mark for a justification that links to why it matters for this specific investigation, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct limitations, each justified with reference to the specific investigation.
- The government survey may not have measured social media use and wellbeing in the same way the researcher defines them [1], so the variables in the secondary data may not align with her research question, reducing validity [1].
- The secondary data was collected at a single point in time or over a period that may not reflect current teenage social media habits [1], which have changed rapidly, reducing the relevance of the conclusions [1].
- The survey may not include all teenagers (not a census) or may have a non-representative sample [1], which would limit how far the conclusions can be generalised [1].
Secure: Two limitations identified, one justified.
Developing: One limitation identified and justified.
Emerging: Names 'secondary data' as a limitation without explaining why.

practice_questions.text:
A news headline claims: 'New study shows people who drink coffee live longer — researchers surveyed 500 coffee drinkers and 500 non-drinkers.'
Discuss the reliability and validity of the conclusions this study can support.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion covering reliability, validity, and potential limitations of the study design.
Mastering: Both reliability and validity addressed with reference to the study design, plus a judgement.
- Reliability concern: a survey measures self-reported coffee consumption, which may vary over time and be inconsistently recalled [1+1].
- Validity concern: the survey measures longevity only in the sample at the point of collection; tracking who lives longest requires a longitudinal study over many years [1+1].
- Confounding/bias: heavy coffee drinkers might share other lifestyle characteristics (higher income, better access to healthcare) that actually explain longevity differences [1+1].
- Judgement: the conclusions are not reliable or valid enough to claim a causal link; the study can only suggest an association that warrants further investigation [1].
Secure: Two of the three threads (reliability, validity, confounding) with partial development.
Developing: One thread with limited development.
Emerging: Describes what the study does without evaluating it.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly defines reliability in statistics?
options: The extent to which a measurement captures what it is supposed to measure
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated
The extent to which the sample represents the population
The extent to which data is free from response bias

knowledge_checks.q: A researcher uses ONS population data for her investigation into UK birth trends. What type of data is this?
options: Primary data collected by field experiment
Secondary data from a reference publication

knowledge_checks.q: Data collected directly by the researcher for the specific purpose of the current investigation is called _____ data.
A bathroom scale that always reads 3 kg too heavy is _____ but not valid.
Match each term to its correct definition:
right: A data collection that includes every member of the population
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated
A systematic distortion that pushes results consistently in one direction

flashcard_questions.a: Reliable but not valid — consistent but inaccurate.

flashcard_questions.q: What is bias in a statistical context?
