glossary_terms.definition: Data collected directly by the researcher for the specific purpose of the current investigation.
Data that already exists, having been collected by someone else for a different purpose.
A data collection that includes every member of the population of interest.
Selecting a subset of the population to collect data from, with the aim of drawing conclusions about the whole population.
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated under the same conditions.
The extent to which a measurement actually measures what it is supposed to measure.
A systematic distortion in data or results that causes them to consistently differ from the true value in a particular direction.

lessons.title: Sampling Methods and Stratification
lessons.description: Choosing a fair sample: random, systematic, stratified-before-sampling, judgement, opportunity and quota.
lessons.content_html:
Why Sampling?

A population is everyone or everything the investigation concerns. But collecting data from every member of a population is often impractical — too expensive, too time-consuming, or simply impossible. Instead, a researcher selects a sample: a manageable subset from which conclusions about the whole population can be drawn.

The quality of those conclusions depends critically on how the sample is selected. A badly chosen sample — one that over-represents some groups and under-represents others — produces biased results. No amount of clever analysis can fix a biased sample. This is why choosing the right sampling method is one of the most important decisions in the planning stage of any investigation.

Before sampling can begin, you need a sample frame: a complete list of everyone in the population. For a school survey, the sample frame might be the roll of all registered students. For a national survey, a sample frame might be the electoral register or postcode address file. The sample frame may not include every member of the population — some individuals are always missed — and this itself can be a source of bias.

Methods That Rely on Judgement or Opportunity

Judgement sampling (also called purposive sampling) is where the researcher deliberately chooses participants they believe are typical. It is fast and avoids obvious outliers, but the researcher’s judgement introduces subjectivity and potential bias. If the researcher’s beliefs about the population are wrong, the sample will be wrong in a systematic way.

Opportunity sampling (also called convenience sampling) means selecting whoever is available. Surveying people who happen to be walking past at a particular time, or asking friends and classmates, are examples. It is the cheapest and fastest method, but it is highly susceptible to bias: the people who are available may systematically differ from the wider population in ways that affect the results.

A sample obtained by opportunity or judgement is not automatically worthless. If you are investigating an exploratory question — trying to identify variables worth studying in more depth — a convenient sample gives a quick first look. In early-stage research, speed can outweigh the need for perfect representativeness.

However, any conclusions drawn from such samples must be clearly caveated: they may not apply to the wider population. The examiner will expect you to state this limitation when evaluating an investigation that used judgement or opportunity sampling.

Random Sampling

In a simple random sample, every member of the population has an equal chance of being included, and selections are made using a genuinely random process. This is the gold standard for avoiding systematic bias: no group is systematically favoured or excluded.

Random selection can be achieved using various techniques, including: assigning numbers to all members of the sample frame and using a random number generator, shuffling a pack of cards, or rolling dice. The specification notes these methods but is explicit: you will not be asked to derive a sample using these techniques in the exam — understanding the principle is what matters.

Systematic Sampling

Systematic sampling selects every ‘k’th member of the sample frame after a random start. For example, to select 20 from a list of 200 people, you calculate k = 200 ÷ 20 = 10, choose a random starting point between 1 and 10, then select every 10th person after that.

Systematic sampling is easier to implement than simple random sampling for large populations, and it spreads the sample evenly across the list. However, it can introduce a hidden pattern if the sample frame itself has a regular structure. If a list alternates male/female and you sample every other entry, you might end up with an all-male or all-female sample.

Key Fact

Systematic sampling steps: (1) calculate the sampling interval k = population size ÷ sample size; (2) choose a random start between 1 and k; (3) select every k-th member after that starting point.

Stratification: Not a Sampling Method

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood ideas in the specification. Stratification is a process that happens before sampling — it is not itself a method of sampling. The specification is explicit: stratification is not a method of sampling but a method which may be used before sampling takes place.

Here is how stratification works: first, you divide the population into meaningful subgroups called strata (singular: stratum) based on a characteristic relevant to the investigation. Then, you select participants from each stratum separately, using a random method, in proportion to the size of each stratum in the population.

Example: a school has 300 students: 120 in Year 10 and 180 in Year 11. You want a sample of 50. If you stratify by year group: Year 10 contributes ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​120/300 × 50 = 20 students; Year 11 contributes 180/300 × 50 = 30 students. Within each stratum, you then select randomly. This ensures the sample reflects the year-group balance of the school.

Key Fact

Stratification divides the population into subgroups BEFORE sampling. The actual sampling method used within each stratum is then random sampling. Calling stratification a “sampling method” is a common error that costs marks.

Quota Sampling (Higher)

Quota sampling looks similar to stratification on the surface: you set a target for each subgroup. But there is a crucial difference. In stratified random sampling, participants within each stratum are chosen randomly. In quota sampling, the researcher fills each quota using whoever is available — there is no random selection within the quota. A market researcher might be told to interview 30 women aged 18–25 and 30 women aged 26–40, but they then choose those 60 participants by opportunity — approaching people in a shopping centre until the quotas are met.

Quota sampling is fast and proportional to the population structure, which is why commercial market research firms often use it. However, because selection within each quota is not random, it is susceptible to the same biases as opportunity sampling. The people a researcher approaches in a shopping centre on a weekday morning systematically differ from those who are at work.

Every sampling method trades off between cost/speed and bias risk. Understanding these trade-offs is what the specification is really testing:

  • Opportunity: Fast, cheap, highly biased. Useful only for pilot/exploratory work.
  • Judgement: Fast, avoids obvious outliers, still subjective. Researcher’s assumptions must be sound.
  • Random: Unbiased in expectation, but requires a complete sample frame and may still miss subgroups by chance in small samples.
  • Systematic: Practical for large populations; watch for hidden patterns in the list.
  • Stratification then random: Best for populations with important subgroups — guarantees proportional representation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error on ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about sampling is calling stratification a sampling method. It is not — it is a pre-sampling division of the population. The sampling happens afterwards, within each stratum, using a random method. If a question asks you to compare two sampling methods, state a numerical comparison where possible (e.g. what proportion of each subgroup would be selected) rather than just describing the method in general terms. On ‘Explain’ questions about bias, name the specific group that would be over- or under-represented, not just “the sample might be biased”.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Opportunity sampling is fast but biased; random sampling is the least biased but requires a complete sample frame; systematic sampling is practical for large populations but can be distorted by patterns in the list.
  • Stratification is a division of the population into subgroups that happens before sampling — it is not itself a sampling method. After stratification, random sampling is applied within each stratum to ensure proportional representation.
  • Every sampling decision is a trade-off between bias and practicality — the exam expects you to explain both what a method does and what its specific bias risks are in context.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes stratification in a statistical investigation?
A) Selecting every fifth person from the sample frame.
B) Choosing participants based on who is most convenient to access.
C) Dividing the population into subgroups before sampling takes place.
D) Setting a quota for each subgroup and filling it using random selection.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — Stratification is the division of the population into subgroups (strata) before sampling, not itself a sampling method.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher wants to select a systematic sample of 40 students from a school roll of 400.
Work out the sampling interval and describe how she should select the first member of the sample.
practice_questions.marks:
Sampling interval k = 400 ÷ 40 = 10 [1 mark].
The first member is chosen randomly from members 1 to 10 (e.g. by generating a random number between 1 and 10) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A school wants to investigate students’ attitudes to homework. There are 180 students in Year 10 and 120 students in Year 11. A stratified sample of 30 students is to be taken.
Calculate the number of Year 10 students and Year 11 students that should be included in the sample.
practice_questions.marks:
Total population = 180 + 120 = 300 [1 mark].
Year 10: 180/300 × 30 = 18 students [1 mark].
Year 11: 120/300 × 30 = 12 students [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why opportunity sampling is considered less reliable than simple random sampling for estimating the average income of adults in a city. Refer to a specific group that might be over- or under-represented.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct issues developed with reference to a specific group.
- Opportunity sampling selects whoever is easiest to reach [1] — for example, surveying people outside a city centre shopping area on a weekday morning would over-represent people who are not in paid employment (e.g. retirees, carers, the unemployed), who may have systematically lower incomes than those at work [1].
- By contrast, simple random sampling gives every adult in the city an equal chance of selection [1], so the sample is not systematically skewed towards any income group [1].
Secure: One issue identified with a specific group named.
Developing: Names the sampling method limitations without a specific group.
Emerging: States 'it is biased' without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
A market research company wants to investigate the TV viewing habits of UK adults. They plan to use opportunity sampling at two shopping centres in Manchester on a Saturday afternoon.
Suggest and justify two improvements to this sampling method that would give a more representative sample of all UK adults.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per improvement and 1 mark per justification that links to a specific representativeness issue, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two improvements, each with a justification referencing who is currently under-represented.
- Collect data from multiple locations across the UK, not just Manchester [1], because residents of one city may differ in viewing habits from those in rural areas or other regions, so the current method under-represents non-urban adults [1].
- Collect data at multiple times of day on different days of the week [1], because people who visit shopping centres on Saturday afternoons may differ from those who work weekends or do not go shopping (e.g. those with disabilities or caring responsibilities), systematically excluding groups with different viewing habits [1].
- Switch to a random or stratified method by obtaining a sample frame (e.g. postcodes) and selecting randomly [1], to give every adult an equal chance of selection and remove the geographic and temporal biases of the current approach [1].
Secure: Two improvements, one justified.
Developing: One improvement with a justification.
Emerging: Describes a change without justifying it.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether stratification before sampling is always preferable to simple random sampling. In your answer, give examples of when each method would be most appropriate.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion with examples and a judgement.
Mastering: Advantages of stratification, advantages of simple random sampling, a comparison of when each applies, and a concluding judgement.
- Stratification advantage: guarantees that key subgroups are proportionally represented — for example, if investigating differences in wellbeing between Year 10 and Year 11 students, stratification ensures both year groups appear in the sample in the right proportions [1+1].
- Stratification disadvantage: requires knowledge of the population’s subgroup structure before sampling; if the researcher does not know the relevant groupings in advance, stratification cannot be applied [1+1].
- Simple random sampling advantage: requires only a complete sample frame and no prior knowledge of subgroups; for homogeneous populations (where subgroups are not relevant), it is just as effective and simpler to implement [1+1].
- Judgement: stratification is preferable when the population has known, relevant subgroups and you want guaranteed representation; simple random sampling is preferable for homogeneous populations or when subgroup structure is unknown [1].
Secure: Two threads addressed with partial development.
Developing: One thread with a relevant example.
Emerging: Describes the methods without comparing them.

knowledge_checks.q: What is a sample frame?
options: The process of dividing a population into subgroups before sampling
The complete list of every member of the population from which a sample can be drawn
The number of people selected in a stratified sample from each stratum
The method used to collect data from each selected participant

knowledge_checks.q: Which statement about stratification is correct?
options: Stratification is a sampling method used to select participants at random
Stratification is used after sampling to group results
Stratification is a method used before sampling to divide the population into subgroups
Stratification is another term for systematic sampling

knowledge_checks.q: In systematic sampling, the researcher selects every k-th member after a _____ starting point.
Selecting participants simply because they are easy to access, with no randomisation, is called _____ sampling.
Match each sampling method to its key characteristic:
right: Every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
Members are selected at regular intervals after a random start
The researcher deliberately selects participants they believe are representative

flashcard_questions.a: A complete list of every member of the population from which a sample is drawn.
flashcard_questions.q: What is a sample frame?

flashcard_questions.a: No. Stratification divides the population into subgroups before sampling takes place.
flashcard_questions.q: Is stratification a sampling method?

flashcard_questions.a: Every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the key feature of a simple random sample?

flashcard_questions.a: Sampling interval = population size divided by required sample size.
flashcard_questions.q: How is the sampling interval calculated in systematic sampling?

flashcard_questions.a: Those available to sample may differ systematically from the wider population.
flashcard_questions.q: What bias risk does opportunity sampling carry?
A school has 200 Year 10 and 100 Year 11 students. A stratified sample of 30 is needed. How many come from Year 11?

flashcard_questions.a: The researcher uses their own judgement to select participants they believe are representative.
flashcard_questions.q: What is judgement sampling?

flashcard_questions.a: Stratification uses random selection within each stratum; quota sampling fills each quota by convenience.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between stratification and quota sampling? (Higher)

flashcard_questions.a: If the sample frame has a repeating pattern, the regular interval may introduce bias.
flashcard_questions.q: What is one potential weakness of systematic sampling?

flashcard_questions.a: To guarantee that important subgroups are represented proportionally in the sample.
flashcard_questions.q: Why might an investigator choose to stratify a population before sampling?

glossary_terms.definition: The complete set of all individuals or items the investigation is about.
A subset of the population selected for data collection, from which conclusions about the whole population are drawn.
A complete list of every member of the population from which a sample can be drawn.
Sampling where the researcher uses their own judgement to select participants they believe are representative of the population.
Sampling where participants are chosen simply because they are convenient or easy to access, without any randomisation.
A sampling method where every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, and selections are made by a random process.
A sampling method where members are selected from the sample frame at regular intervals, after a random starting point.
Dividing a population into distinct subgroups (strata) based on a shared characteristic, before sampling takes place.
A sampling method where the researcher sets a target number (quota) for each subgroup and then fills each quota using any convenient means.

lessons.title: Questionnaires, Pilot Studies and Cleaning Data
lessons.description: Designing fair questions, running a pilot, and cleaning a messy raw dataset before analysis begins.
lessons.content_html:
Designing a Good Questionnaire

A questionnaire is only as good as the questions it contains. Even with a perfect sample, a poorly designed questionnaire will produce data that is biased, incomplete, or simply not measuring what you intended. The specification identifies several key features to consider: leading questions, avoiding biased sources, the choice of open or closed questions, interview technique, and time factors.

Leading Questions

A leading question nudges the respondent towards a particular answer. Consider these two versions:

  • Leading: “Don’t you agree that students should do at least one hour of exercise a day?”
  • Neutral: “How many hours of exercise do you do on a typical day?”

The first version makes it socially awkward to disagree. Respondents who exercise very little may inflate their answers to avoid seeming lazy. The second makes no assumption. Always ask: does this question imply there is a right or preferred answer? If yes, rewrite it.

Which of these is leading? Think before reading on.

  • 1. “How often do you eat unhealthy food?” — Leading. The word “unhealthy” primes the respondent to under-report.
  • 2. “What type of food do you eat most often?” — Not leading. No assumption is built in.
  • 3. “Most young people spend too much time on their phones. How many hours do you spend on your phone per day?” — Leading. The preamble sets an expectation that shapes the answer.

Open and Closed Questions

Open questions invite free-text answers. The response might be detailed and revealing, but every answer is different — comparing many different written opinions requires careful judgement rather than straightforward statistical analysis.

Closed questions provide fixed options. The data is straightforward to count and compare. Always check that closed-question options are exhaustive (they cover all possible answers) and mutually exclusive (no answer fits more than one option).

Key Fact

Open questions: rich detail but hard to analyse statistically. Closed questions: easy to count and compare but may not capture every possible view. Good questionnaires often use both types.

Interview Technique and Time Factors

The way an interview is conducted can affect responses. Face-to-face interviews allow clarification of confusing questions, but the interviewer’s presence can cause socially desirable answers. Telephone or online questionnaires offer more anonymity, which may encourage more honest responses on sensitive topics, though response rates are often lower.

Time factors matter too. Asking about sleep habits on a Monday (after a weekend) will produce different answers from asking mid-week. Seasonal effects can skew data about outdoor activities, mental wellbeing, or energy consumption. A good questionnaire design considers when the questions will be asked and whether timing could bias the results.

Pilot Studies

A pilot study is a small-scale practice run — you administer the questionnaire to a small group before the main data collection. It serves several purposes:

  • Identifying ambiguous or unclear questions that respondents interpret differently.
  • Checking that response categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
  • Estimating how long the questionnaire takes, so respondents can be informed.
  • Revealing leading or loaded language the researcher did not notice when writing the questions.

The pilot participants are typically not included in the main investigation. After the pilot, the questionnaire is revised before real data collection begins. Skipping the pilot is a common planning mistake — it is far cheaper to fix problems before 500 responses are collected than afterwards.

Cleaning Data

Raw data is rarely perfect. Before analysis begins, the dataset must be cleaned — checked and corrected for errors and inconsistencies. The specification identifies several types of problem that require data cleaning:

Missing data: Some respondents skip questions. A missing value cannot be included in calculations — you must decide whether to exclude the incomplete response, impute a value, or note the gap and acknowledge the effect on your results.

Non-responses: The entire questionnaire is not returned. If non-respondents share a characteristic, excluding them introduces bias.

Incorrect formats: A question asking for age might receive “sixteen” (text) alongside numerical entries. Spreadsheet software cannot calculate with inconsistent formats, so these must be standardised.

Extraneous notation: Currency symbols, spaces, or units entered inconsistently (“£4500” vs “4500” vs “4,500”) will prevent calculations. These must be removed or standardised before analysis.

Key Fact

Three main data cleaning problems: (1) missing data — blank cells where responses were skipped; (2) incorrect formats — inconsistent data entry; (3) extraneous notation — symbols or punctuation that prevent calculation.

Spotting Errors Using Row and Column Totals

One practical cleaning technique is to check whether values in a row or column are internally consistent. If the row total for a group is 45 but the three individual entries sum to 50, one entry is wrong. The specification notes that students may be asked to use row or column totals to identify a wrongly recorded value.

A worked example: a table records the number of books read by students in three year groups over two terms. If Year 9’s Term 1 column total is 120 but the individual class entries are 42, 38, and 45 (summing to 125), one of these three entries has been incorrectly recorded and needs investigating.

Control Groups and Extraneous Variables (Higher)

When an investigation compares two groups — for example, students who received a new study intervention versus those who did not — the group that does not receive the treatment is the control group. Without a control group, you cannot know whether any improvement is due to the intervention or would have happened anyway.

Extraneous variables — factors that could influence the outcome but are not the variable being tested — must be identified and held constant where possible. For example, if testing whether music helps concentration, room temperature and time of day are extraneous variables that should be kept the same across both groups.

An incomplete response is one where a participant returns the questionnaire but leaves some questions blank — perhaps because a question was unclear or felt too personal. A non-response is where the questionnaire is not returned at all.

Both create gaps in the data. Incomplete responses might be rescued for the questions that were answered, whereas non-responses produce no usable data. In both cases, if those affected share a characteristic, the results are biased.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about questionnaire design, a common error is giving a vague improvement such as “make the questions clearer”. You must identify the specific problem (e.g. “the question is leading because it implies one answer is preferred”) and the specific improvement (e.g. “rewrite as a neutral question with no implied preferred answer”). For data cleaning questions where a table is given, show your working: add up the row or column to demonstrate where the inconsistency lies.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Leading questions introduce bias by implying a preferred answer; closed questions produce data that is easier to analyse but must have exhaustive, mutually exclusive options; open questions produce richer but harder-to-analyse responses.
  • A pilot study is a small-scale trial run that identifies ambiguities, errors, and timing issues before the main data collection begins — skipping it risks finding problems when it is too late to fix them.
  • Raw data must be cleaned before analysis: missing values, incorrect formats, extraneous notation, and data entry errors identifiable by checking row and column totals must all be addressed before any statistical measures are calculated.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a leading question?
A) How many hours of sleep do you get on a typical school night?
B) Do you agree that teenagers need more sleep than adults?
C) At what time do you usually go to bed on weekdays?
D) How many times did you wake up during the night last week?
practice_questions.marks: B [1 mark] — Uses 'Do you agree that...' which implies a correct answer and primes respondents to agree.

practice_questions.text:
A student is cleaning a dataset and notices that in a table of test scores, the three entries for Group B are 24, 31, and 19, but the column total is listed as 78.
Work out whether the column total is correct, and if not, identify the discrepancy.
practice_questions.marks:
24 + 31 + 19 = 74 [1 mark].
The column total of 78 is incorrect; there is a discrepancy of 4 marks [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A researcher designs the following question for a survey: 'Most health experts recommend eating five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. How many portions did you eat yesterday?'
Describe one problem with this question and explain how it could be improved.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for identifying the problem and 2 marks for a developed explanation with an improvement.
Problem: the preamble about health experts is leading [1] because it sets a social norm (five portions) that respondents may feel they should meet, causing overstatement [1].
Improvement: remove the preamble and ask simply 'How many portions of fruit and vegetables did you eat yesterday?' so no expected answer is implied [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a pilot study should be carried out before collecting the main data in an investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per reason, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct reasons, each with a developed explanation.
- Ambiguous questions: the pilot reveals whether respondents interpret questions consistently [1]; if different people read the same question differently, the data will measure different things, undermining validity [1].
- Response categories: the pilot checks whether closed-question options are exhaustive [1]; if a common response is missing from the options, respondents force their answer into an ill-fitting category, producing inaccurate data [1].
- Timing: the pilot estimates completion time [1]; if the questionnaire takes much longer than expected, response rates in the main study will fall [1].
Secure: Two reasons, one developed. Developing: One reason with limited development. Emerging: States 'to check it works' without a developed reason.

practice_questions.text:
A class investigation asks 80 students to rate how often they exercise using the scale: Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always. After collection, 15 questionnaires have at least one blank response and 8 students did not return their questionnaire at all.
Suggest and justify two ways the investigator should handle these data issues before calculating any statistical measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per suggestion and 1 mark per justification linked to a specific data quality issue, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two strategies, each justified.
- For questionnaires with some blank responses: include them for the questions that were answered, excluding only specific missing values [1]; this preserves as much data as possible rather than wasting the partially complete response [1].
- For non-responses: note the 8 non-responders (out of 88) and consider whether they share a characteristic [1]; if less active students were less motivated to return the form, results will overestimate exercise frequency [1].
- Standardise coding: assign numerical codes consistently (1=Never to 5=Always) [1] so the same response is treated identically in every calculation [1].
Secure: Two strategies, one justified. Developing: One strategy with a justification. Emerging: Names missing data without suggesting how to handle it.

practice_questions.text:
A student is designing a questionnaire about students' diets. She includes the question: 'How many portions of fruit and vegetables do you eat? 0-2 / 3-4 / 5-7 / 7-10.'
Discuss at least two problems with this questionnaire design and suggest how each could be improved.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for identified problems with developments and specific improvements.
Mastering: Two or more distinct problems identified and developed, each with a clear improvement and a judgement.
- Overlapping categories: '5-7' and '7-10' both include 7, so a respondent who eats exactly 7 portions does not know which to choose [1]; correct by making categories mutually exclusive: 0-2 / 3-4 / 5-7 / 8-10 [1].
- No 'more than' option: a student eating 11 or more portions cannot fit into any category [1]; add '10 or more' to make options exhaustive [1].
- Vague period: 'how many portions' does not specify a time frame [1]; add 'on a typical day' to standardise the reference period [1].
- Judgement: multiple design errors in one question will produce data that cannot be reliably analysed or compared across respondents [1].
Secure: Two problems, one developed improvement. Developing: One problem with an improvement. Emerging: Names the problem type without explaining what it means.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the main purpose of a pilot study?
options: To collect the main dataset before the full investigation begins
To select the sampling method that will be used
To trial the questionnaire on a small group and identify problems before the main data collection
To clean the data after it has been collected

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a leading question?
options: A question with more than four response options
A question that is worded to steer the respondent towards a particular answer
A question with no fixed response options
A question that is asked at the start of the survey

knowledge_checks.q: A closed question provides a fixed set of response options that must be _____ (covering all possible answers) and mutually exclusive.
Data that includes symbols, inconsistent units, or incorrectly formatted entries needs to be _____ before analysis.
Match each data quality issue to its correct description:
right: Blank cells where a participant skipped a question
Inconsistent data entry that software cannot process
An entire questionnaire not returned by the participant

glossary_terms.definition: A question that is worded in a way that steers the respondent towards a particular answer, introducing bias into the data.
Questions that allow the respondent to answer in their own words, producing qualitative data that is rich but harder to analyse statistically.
Questions that provide a fixed set of response options for the respondent to choose from, producing data that is easier to analyse statistically.
A small-scale trial run of a questionnaire or data collection method, conducted before the main investigation to identify and fix problems.
A group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment being tested, used as a baseline to measure the effect of the treatment.
Variables that influence the response variable but are not the focus of the investigation and must be identified and controlled.
